questions.title: A congenital, unchanging, reddish chest nodule in a teenager is a hemangioma
questions.question: 14-year-old healthy girl has a 0.3 cm reddish, slightly raised nodule on the skin of the upper part of her chest found on a routine physical examination. She states that this lesion has been present since birth and has not appreciably changed in size or color. Which of the following neoplasms is this nodule most likely to be?
questions.vignette: A 14-year-old healthy girl has a 0.3 cm reddish, slightly raised chest-skin nodule present since birth, unchanged in size or colour.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Melanoma is a malignant tumour of melanocytes that would be expected to grow, change colour or shape over time, not remain stable and unchanged since birth.
explanations.B: Correct. A small, reddish, raised skin nodule present since birth and unchanged in size or colour describes a haemangioma, a benign tumour of blood vessels (a vascular birthmark). Its congenital onset and long-term stability are the key features distinguishing it from a malignant, acquired or progressively changing lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumour, typically acquired later in life and progressively enlarging, not a stable congenital vascular nodule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lymphoma is a malignant tumour of lymphoid tissue, not a congenital vascular skin birthmark.

questions.subtopic: Hemangioma as a benign congenital vascular tumour
questions.learning_objective: Recognise a stable congenital reddish skin nodule as a haemangioma.

questions.title: A soft, painless, stable forearm mass is a lipoma
questions.question: A 27-year-old woman in excellent health has a routine health maintenance examination. A 2 cm soft, rounded mass is palpable beneath the skin of the left forearm. She has no difficulty using the arm and there is no associated pain with the mass, either in movement or on palpation. The overlying skin appears normal. The mass does not change in size over the next year. Which of the following neoplasms is she most likely to have?
questions.vignette: A healthy 27-year-old woman has a 2 cm soft, rounded, painless subcutaneous forearm mass, normal overlying skin, stable over a year of follow-up.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant skeletal-muscle tumour that would be expected to grow and cause symptoms, not remain a stable, painless, soft mass over a year.
explanations.B: Correct. A soft, rounded, painless, slow-growing subcutaneous mass with normal overlying skin is the classic presentation of a lipoma. Lipoma is a benign tumour of mature adipose tissue, the most common soft-tissue tumour overall. It is typically found incidentally and, as here, remains stable in size over time.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Melanoma is a malignant pigmented skin lesion, not a soft, non-pigmented, subcutaneous mass.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Metastatic carcinoma would present as a growing, often firm and irregular mass reflecting an underlying malignancy elsewhere, not a stable benign-feeling soft mass in an otherwise healthy young woman.

questions.subtopic: Lipoma as a benign, soft, stable subcutaneous fatty tumour
questions.learning_objective: Recognise a soft, painless, stable subcutaneous mass as a lipoma.

questions.title: A hair- and cartilage-containing cystic ovarian mass is a teratoma
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman has noted dull pelvic pain for the last two months. On physical examination there is a mass palpated in the right lower quadrant. An abdominal ultrasound reveals an 8 cm mass involving the right ovary. The mass is surgically excised. On gross inspection, the surface of the mass is smooth and is not adherent to surrounding pelvic structure. On sectioning it is cystic and filled with hair. On microscopic examination there is squamous epithelium, tall columnar glandular epithelium, cartilage, and fibrous connective tissue. Which of the following neoplasms is she most likely to have?
questions.vignette: A 32-year-old woman has an 8 cm right ovarian mass, smooth and non-adherent, cystic and hair-filled on sectioning, with squamous epithelium, glandular epithelium, cartilage and fibrous connective tissue on microscopy.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A choristoma is normal tissue found in an abnormal (ectopic) location, not a neoplasm composed of tissues from all three germ layers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A myxoma is a benign tumour of primitive mesenchymal (connective) tissue with abundant myxoid stroma, not one composed of squamous epithelium, glandular epithelium and cartilage together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A hamartoma is a disorganised overgrowth of mature tissue elements normal to the site, not a tumour derived from all three germ layers.
explanations.D: Correct. A cystic ovarian mass containing hair, along with squamous epithelium (ectoderm), glandular epithelium (endoderm) and cartilage/fibrous connective tissue (mesoderm), demonstrates tissue derived from all three germ layers. This mixture of three-germ-layer tissue is the defining feature of a teratoma. Here it presents as a mature cystic teratoma, also called a dermoid cyst, of the ovary.

questions.subtopic: Teratoma as a tumour of all three germ layers
questions.learning_objective: Recognise an ovarian mass with hair, squamous epithelium, glandular epithelium and cartilage as a teratoma.

questions.title: A slow-growing, solid, circumscribed uterine nodule is a leiomyoma
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman had a firm nodule palpable on the dome of the uterus six years ago recorded on routine physical examination. The nodule has slowly increased in size and now appears to be about twice the size it was when first discovered. By ultrasound scan it is solid and circumscribed. She remains asymptomatic. Which of the following neoplasms is she most likely to have?
questions.vignette: A 35-year-old woman has a firm uterine-dome nodule, present for 6 years, slowly doubled in size, solid and circumscribed on ultrasound, asymptomatic.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leiomyosarcoma is the malignant counterpart, which typically grows faster and more aggressively, unlike this slow (6-year) doubling course.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hemangioma is a benign vascular tumour, not the typical benign smooth-muscle tumour that produces a firm, solid, circumscribed uterine nodule of this kind.
explanations.C: Correct. A firm, solid, well-circumscribed, slow-growing uterine nodule is the classic presentation of a leiomyoma, also called a uterine fibroid. Leiomyoma is the benign tumour of uterine smooth muscle, extremely common, typically asymptomatic, and growing very slowly over years. This matches the 6-year, slowly-doubling course described here exactly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adenocarcinoma is a malignant glandular epithelial tumour, not the smooth-muscle-derived firm nodule described here, and would not typically remain circumscribed and slow-growing over 6 years.

questions.subtopic: Leiomyoma as a benign, slow-growing uterine smooth-muscle tumour
questions.learning_objective: Recognise a firm, solid, circumscribed, slow-growing uterine nodule as a leiomyoma.

questions.title: Chondroma is the benign tumour of cartilage
questions.question: Benign tumor of cartilage is called an:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipoma is the benign tumour of adipose (fat) tissue, not cartilage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leiomyoma is the benign tumour of smooth muscle, not cartilage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteoma is the benign tumour of bone (osseous) tissue, not cartilage.
explanations.D: Correct. Chondroma is the benign tumour of cartilage. It follows the standard mesenchymal-tumour naming convention, in which a benign tumour is named after its tissue of origin plus the suffix '-oma'. Here the origin is cartilage, giving 'chondro-oma'.

questions.subtopic: Chondroma as the benign cartilage tumour
questions.learning_objective: Name chondroma as the benign tumour of cartilage.

questions.title: Osteoma is the benign tumour of osseous tissue
questions.question: Benign tumor of osseous tissue is called an:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipoma is the benign tumour of adipose (fat) tissue, not bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leiomyoma is the benign tumour of smooth muscle, not bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chondroma is the benign tumour of cartilage, not osseous (bone) tissue specifically.
explanations.D: Correct. Osteoma is the benign tumour of osseous, i.e. bone, tissue. It follows the same standard mesenchymal-tumour naming convention as chondroma and lipoma. Here the tissue of origin is bone, giving 'osteo-oma'.

questions.subtopic: Osteoma as the benign osseous tumour
questions.learning_objective: Name osteoma as the benign tumour of osseous tissue.

questions.title: Hamartoma is a mass of disorganised but mature native tissue
questions.question: Hamartoma refers to:

options.A: Mass of disorganised but mature cells indigenous to the part
options.C: Tumour differentiating towards more than one cell line
options.D: Mass of ectopic rests of normal tissue

explanations.A: Correct. A hamartoma is a mass of disorganised, but otherwise mature and histologically normal, cells and tissue elements. Those elements are indigenous, or native, to the part of the body in which it occurs. It is a developmental malformation of local tissue architecture rather than a true, clonal neoplasm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A tumour arising from totipotent cells (able to give rise to any tissue type, including extra-embryonic tissue) describes a germ-cell tumour, not a hamartoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A tumour differentiating towards more than one cell line derived from all three germ layers describes a teratoma, not a hamartoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A mass of ectopic rests of normal tissue -- normal tissue in an abnormal location -- describes a choristoma, the entity hamartoma is classically distinguished from (hamartoma: native tissue, disorganised; choristoma: normal tissue, wrong location).

questions.subtopic: Hamartoma definition versus choristoma, germ-cell tumour and teratoma
questions.learning_objective: Define hamartoma as a mass of disorganised but mature, native tissue.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Mass of disorganised but mature cells indigenous to the part"

questions.title: Malignant glandular tumours are called adenocarcinoma
questions.question: Malignant tumours are:

options.A: When arising from glandular cells are called adenocarcinoma
options.D: When arising from epithelial cells are called sarcomas

explanations.A: Correct. When a malignant tumour arises from glandular epithelial cells, it is named adenocarcinoma. This is the same naming fact tested elsewhere in this lecture set for carcinoma of glands, restated here as the general defining statement about malignant tumour nomenclature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Malignant tumours are not defined as well differentiated; differentiation ranges from well to poorly differentiated (graded I-IV), and many malignant tumours are poorly differentiated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malignant tumours are defined by their capacity to metastasise (spread to distant sites), not by rarely doing so; metastasis is a hallmark malignant feature, not an exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A malignant tumour arising from epithelial cells is called a carcinoma, not a sarcoma -- sarcoma specifically denotes a malignant tumour of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin.

questions.learning_objective: State that a malignant tumour arising from glandular cells is called adenocarcinoma.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: When arising from glandular cells are called adenocarcinoma"
field_notes.reuse: Reuses this batch's own Lecture 49 adenocarcinoma concept CON-FND-493ABE0143A7CD -- identical naming fact, restated as the general nomenclature statement.

questions.title: Sarcomas are not made of masses and sheets of malignant cells
questions.question: Sarcomas are NOT characterized by:

options.C: Made of masses and sheets of malignant cells

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. sarcomas ARE characterized by this). Sarcomas commonly show areas of haemorrhage and necrosis, especially in rapidly growing, poorly vascularised regions.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. sarcomas ARE characterized by this). Sarcomas are known for common local recurrence after excision, reflecting their infiltrative growth pattern.
explanations.C: Correct (i.e. sarcomas are NOT characterized by this, the exception). Growth as masses and sheets of malignant cells is the cohesive growth pattern of carcinoma, whose epithelial cells stick together in nests and sheets. Sarcoma cells, by contrast, are typically dispersed as individual cells separated by abundant connective-tissue stroma -- the same stromal-relationship fact tested elsewhere in this lecture set -- so 'masses and sheets' is specifically not how sarcomas are described.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. sarcomas ARE characterized by this). Sarcomas usually attain large sizes before detection, since they often arise in deep soft tissue without early symptoms.

questions.subtopic: Sarcoma growth pattern not masses/sheets (restates the stroma-separation fact)
questions.learning_objective: Recognise that sarcomas are not characterized by growth as cohesive masses and sheets of malignant cells, unlike carcinomas.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Made of masses and sheets of malignant cells"
field_notes.reuse: Reuses this batch's own Lecture 49 sarcoma-vs-carcinoma-stroma concept CON-FND-EBC323671C0727 -- same underlying fact, framed here as an EXCEPT question.

questions.title: Teratoma is the benign tumour derived from all 3 germ cell layers
questions.question: What is a benign tumor called that is derived from all 3 germ cell layer

explanations.A: Correct. Teratoma is the tumour derived from all three germ cell layers -- ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm -- the same defining fact tested with a clinical vignette earlier in this lecture set (the hair- and cartilage-containing ovarian mass). A mature teratoma is benign; an immature teratoma, containing embryonic-appearing tissue, is malignant.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphoma is a malignant tumour of lymphoid tissue, a single lineage, not a tumour of all three germ layers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibroma is a benign tumour of fibrous connective tissue, a single mesenchymal lineage, not all three germ layers.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myoma is a benign tumour of muscle tissue, a single mesenchymal lineage, not all three germ layers.

questions.subtopic: Teratoma as a tumour of all three germ layers (restated)
questions.learning_objective: Identify teratoma as the tumour derived from all three germ cell layers.

field_notes.reuse: Reuses q422's teratoma concept CON-FND-CB60542E06A0C6 -- same underlying fact restated as a direct definition question.

questions.title: Haematoma is not a benign tumour
questions.question: Which is Not a benign tumour:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. papilloma IS a benign tumour). Papilloma is a genuine benign neoplasm of non-glandular epithelium.
explanations.B: Correct (i.e. haematoma is NOT a benign tumour, the exception). A haematoma is a localised collection of extravasated blood outside blood vessels, caused by bleeding into tissue -- a reactive, non-neoplastic process, not a true clonal neoplasm at all, despite the name's superficial resemblance to a tumour suffix.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. adenoma IS a benign tumour). Adenoma is a genuine benign neoplasm of glandular epithelium.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. fibroma IS a benign tumour). Fibroma is a genuine benign neoplasm of fibrous connective tissue.

questions.subtopic: Haematoma as a non-neoplastic blood collection, not a benign tumour
questions.learning_objective: Recognise haematoma as a non-neoplastic blood collection rather than a true benign tumour.
